title: Accurate Failure Prediction in Agents Does Not Imply Effective Failure Prevention
history: Submission history From: Melisa Russak [ view email ] [v1] Tue, 3 Feb 2026 10:02:50 UTC (247 KB)
status: arXiv preprint; peer review not independently confirmed
verification: Primary metadata plus full-text method/results reading; not independently reproduced
summary: A binary critic scores live prefixes; temperature scaling adjusts confidence before rollback or appended guidance. The study separates recovery of otherwise failing runs from disruption of otherwise successful ones, and uses a 50-task pilot to predict whether deployment will help.
findings: Offline AUROC 0.94 coexists with a 26-percentage-point success collapse in one setting; high-failure ALFWorld gains 2.8 points. Outcomes depend on the backbone and baseline success rate.
design: Task-disjoint train/validation/test partitions; ALFWorld is absent from critic training. Intervention sweeps and heuristic controls support a deployment comparison rather than only offline classification.
gap: The predictor-to-policy distinction is already demonstrated. Two simple intervention modes do not identify a general action-specific optimal policy; a global go/no-go pilot is narrower than local benefit estimation.
future: Estimate action-specific net benefit with replicated checkpoint branches, and test confidence-bound decisions against a fixed threshold at equal total budget.
role: Principal conceptual baseline; prevents an AUROC-only novelty claim.
evidence_location: Sections on critic calibration, intervention results, pilot test, and limitations.

title: Fail-Fast, Restart-Smart: Early Failure Prediction and Restart for SWE Agentic Tasks

status: arXiv preprint; peer review not independently confirmed

summary: A 0.6B black-box monitor learns terminal and dense fail-to-pass supervision from observable prefixes. An alarm starts a same-policy run with a clean prompt history. Stable partial edits are offered as an optional diff, so the new attempt can inspect, apply, or reject them.
findings: At a target 5% false-positive rate, transferred monitoring saves 14.6–20.4% execution tokens. At a 25% target, Qwen resolution rises from 66.6% to 71.8%, versus 66.8% for cold restart. The higher-success operating point adds net token cost.

gap: Transfer can succeed: PreAct cannot claim all monitors fail across agents. Restart and artifact reuse are established; a fixed restart policy does not learn which feasible intervention is best.
future: Compare monitor representations on identical traces and budgets; add verification and abstention controls, reporting any overhead beyond saved execution tokens.
evidence_location: Experimental setup, threshold calibration, Tables on stopping and restart, deployment limitations.

title: PrefixGuard: Online Failure Warning and Trace-Grounded Diagnosis for LLM Agents

title: When Evidence is Sparse: Weakly Supervised Early Failure Alerting in Dialogs and LLM-Agent Trajectories

domain: Dialog, support, tool use and planning
summary: An attention model learns which turns carry failure evidence from terminal labels instead of labeling every prefix equally. A preference-conditioned alpha-STOP policy chooses an accuracy–earliness operating point without retraining a separate trigger for each preference.
findings: Across five benchmarks, relevant evidence occupies 4.7–11.3% of turns and first appears after 59.0–83.6% of trajectories on average. Predictor frontier hypervolume improves 1–10%; the combined system improves 3–42% over compared triggers.

evidence_location: Evidence-sparsity analysis, predictor/trigger experiments, limitations.

evidence_location: Dataset and attribution comparisons; inspected camera-ready v3.

title: Why Do Multi-Agent LLM Systems Fail?
history: Submission history From: Mert Cemri [ view email ] [v1] Mon, 17 Mar 2025 19:04:38 UTC (4,636 KB) [v2] Tue, 22 Apr 2025 18:37:24 UTC (5,814 KB) [v3] Sun, 26 Oct 2025 23:25:18 UTC (653 KB)
status: arXiv preprint; peer review not independently confirmed; source record: ArXiv v3
verification: Primary metadata plus full-text method/results reading; not independently reproduced
summary: Expert analysis of 150 traces yields fourteen failure modes grouped into system design, inter-agent misalignment and task verification. A validated judge scales annotations across a larger multi-agent corpus.
findings: MAST-Data contains over 1,600 traces. Reported expert agreement is kappa 0.88; failures often reflect coordination and verification rather than one isolated model error.
design: This is an empirical taxonomy, not a prospective predictor. Annotator agreement measures label consistency, not causal validity or monitor recall.
gap: Failure categories can guide features but do not provide prevention windows. System-level causes may not be attributable to one recoverable local action.
future: Annotate when each mode first becomes observable and test interventions specific to coordination versus capability versus verification failures.
role: Failure modes and multi-agent feature design.
evidence_location: Taxonomy construction, annotation validation and cross-framework analysis.

title: Failure as a Process: An Anatomy of CLI Coding Agent Trajectories
history: Submission history From: Xiangxin Zhao [ view email ] [v1] Fri, 10 Jul 2026 15:25:56 UTC (843 KB)
status: arXiv preprint; peer review not independently confirmed; source record: 12 pages, 6 figures
verification: Primary metadata plus full-text method/results reading; not independently reproduced
summary: The study treats coding failure as a developing sequence of decisions and observations rather than only a final unresolved patch. It analyzes recurring phases and behavioral patterns in CLI-agent traces.
findings: Of 3,843 traces from seven frontier models and three scaffolds on Terminal-Bench, 1,794 valid complete traces (over 63,000 steps) receive manual annotation. Fourteen findings indicate predominantly epistemic errors, often beginning early but becoming visible late.
design: A retrospective trajectory study can associate behaviors with outcome without demonstrating that those features are visible early or causally repairable.
gap: Patterns can reflect scaffold logging, task difficulty or selection on final outcome. A descriptive association does not establish an online risk score.
future: Freeze prefix-only features from its taxonomy, test task/agent holdouts, and validate candidate mechanisms with controlled edits to the execution policy.
evidence_location: Empirical setup, trajectory analyses and limitations; findings refined from full-text extraction.

title: From Plan to Action: How Well Do Agents Follow the Plan?
history: Submission history From: Saman Dehghan [ view email ] [v1] Mon, 13 Apr 2026 23:54:55 UTC (11,307 KB) [v2] Tue, 28 Apr 2026 15:58:17 UTC (11,307 KB) [v3] Fri, 7 Aug 2026 02:49:47 UTC (15,520 KB)
status: arXiv preprint; peer review not independently confirmed
verification: Primary metadata plus full-text method/results reading; not independently reproduced
summary: The paper compares declared plans with subsequent actions, analyzing how plan quality, reminders and execution choices affect programming-agent behavior. It supplies evidence for plan deviation as a candidate monitor signal.
findings: The inspected v3 analyzes 21,120 SWE-agent trajectories across four models, two SWE benchmarks and eight plan variations. Standard plans and reminders help in evaluated settings; subpar plans and some added early phases hurt. Older bibliography counts are superseded.
design: Plan generation and reminders are evaluated as agent-policy interventions. A deviation may be beneficial adaptation to new evidence, so compliance labels require context.
gap: A strict plan-deviation feature risks false alarms when the original plan is wrong. Plans differ in granularity and scaffold presentation.
future: Separate justified revision from unexplained drift, and test whether a deviation signal predicts added verification value beyond tool errors and task difficulty.
role: Plan-deviation feature backing with a target-mismatch caution.
evidence_location: Plan/action assessment, reminder experiment and threats to validity.

title: Abduct, Act, Predict: Scaffolding Causal Inference for Automated Failure Attribution in Multi-Agent Systems
history: Submission history From: Yixuan Weng [ view email ] [v1] Fri, 12 Sep 2025 16:51:15 UTC (428 KB) [v2] Tue, 23 Sep 2025 14:45:53 UTC (747 KB)
status: arXiv preprint; peer review not independently confirmed
verification: Primary metadata plus full-text method/results reading; not independently reproduced
summary: A single LLM inference is scaffolded to abduct hidden causes, propose a minimal correction and imagine the subsequent trajectory. Full conversation context supports causal-style reasoning, without requiring actual environment execution of the imagined branch.
findings: Step accuracy is 47.46% versus 16.67% on 126 algorithm-generated cases, and 29.31% versus 12.07% on 58 hand-crafted cases. These are attribution results, not measured rescue rates.
design: The correction and outcome are mentally simulated inside the model. This is not an executable interventional identification design, despite causal terminology.
gap: Causal-style prompting is already established. Imagined outcomes can be wrong; PreAct must distinguish hypothetical attribution from actual branch execution and randomization.
future: Reuse active hypothesis verification in live prefixes, recording legality, replayability and downstream outcome for each intervention.
evidence_location: Abduct/act/predict framework and attribution evaluation.

title: DoVer: Intervention-Driven Auto Debugging for LLM Multi-Agent Systems
history: Submission history From: Ming Ma [ view email ] [v1] Sun, 7 Dec 2025 09:23:48 UTC (2,348 KB) [v2] Tue, 9 Dec 2025 13:22:36 UTC (2,247 KB) [v3] Sat, 31 Jan 2026 03:48:05 UTC (2,248 KB)
status: arXiv preprint; peer review not independently confirmed
verification: Primary metadata plus full-text method/results reading; not independently reproduced
summary: Failure hypotheses are tested by targeted interventions such as changing a plan or editing a message. Outcome progress replaces a single responsible-step label, because distinct repairs may independently solve the same failed task.
findings: Reported recovery is 18–28% on failed GAIA/AssistantBench trials, with up to 16% milestone progress and 30–60% of hypotheses validated/refuted; AG2/GSMPlus recovery is 49%.
design: These are conditional failed-trial recovery rates, not population success gains. Cross-framework evidence supports debugging portability but does not establish a frozen predictive monitor.
gap: Outcome-oriented and intervention-validated debugging are established. Recovery after completed failure does not choose an early beneficial interruption point.
future: Compare diagnostic interventions at matched live checkpoints and include untouched successful runs to estimate disruption and net utility.
evidence_location: Framework, dataset-specific recovery and hypothesis-validation results.

title: Where LLM Agents Fail and How They can Learn From Failures
history: Submission history From: Kunlun Zhu [ view email ] [v1] Mon, 29 Sep 2025 18:20:27 UTC (4,063 KB)
status: arXiv preprint; peer review not independently confirmed
verification: Primary metadata plus full-text method/results reading; not independently reproduced
target: Failure explanation and learning from feedback
summary: A failure-analysis framework organizes recurring agent errors and converts diagnoses into feedback intended to improve subsequent execution. The work connects error analysis with corrective agent behavior.
findings: AgentErrorBench spans ALFWorld, GAIA and WebShop. Average all-correct attribution rises from 0.3% to 24.3%, and exact step accuracy from 28% to 45%. Iterative targeted feedback improves task success by up to 26% relative, not 26 percentage points.
design: Diagnosis and feedback may use completed trajectories. Their availability at a proposed action must be checked before using them as online features.
gap: Improving later attempts is different from rescuing the current run. Fault labels can mix local symptoms with upstream causes.
future: Evaluate masked-prefix feedback, compare to simple reflection/retry, and retain a same-policy resampling control.
evidence_location: Failure taxonomy, AgentDebug framework and benchmark experiments.

title: TRAIL: Trace Reasoning and Agentic Issue Localization

summary: A trace-based benchmark evaluates how well models identify and explain agentic execution issues. It provides structured error-analysis tasks and a reusable setting for diagnostic reasoning.
findings: TRAIL contains 148 human-annotated traces from single- and multi-agent systems. The reported best Gemini-2.5-Pro score is 11%; this benchmark score is not warning accuracy or failure AUROC.
design: Post-hoc issue analysis can see information that a live monitor cannot. Its labeled unit is an issue in a trace, rather than an independent task-level intervention outcome.
gap: Trace reasoning quality does not show early detection or recovery value. Errors may be valid labels without a unique intervention point.
future: Build prefix masks and success controls, then use executable checks to test whether the identified issue is actionable.
evidence_location: Benchmark construction and model localization evaluation.

title: AgentNoiseBench: Benchmarking Robustness of Tool-Using LLM Agents Under Noisy Condition
history: Submission history From: Ruipeng Wang [ view email ] [v1] Wed, 11 Feb 2026 20:33:10 UTC (14,511 KB) [v2] Wed, 18 Feb 2026 01:36:58 UTC (14,755 KB)
status: arXiv preprint; peer review not independently confirmed
verification: Primary metadata plus full-text method/results reading; not independently reproduced
summary: The benchmark perturbs the external conditions faced by tool agents and evaluates robustness. It separates environmental noise from reasoning capability and exposes how corrupted observations affect execution.
findings: The study distinguishes user noise from tool noise and preserves task solvability during injection. Its primary comparison reports an average accuracy drop of 20.8% under noise; the measure is task accuracy, not monitor discrimination.
design: Controlled noise permits systematic stress tests. Perturbation realism, severity and dependence on tool schemas limit extrapolation to organic failures.
gap: Noise sensitivity is not an online alarm policy. A monitor can spuriously learn injection artifacts rather than semantic contradiction.
future: Evaluate intervention policies on both injected and naturally noisy runs, and compare tool-contract checks with semantic inconsistency scores.
role: Stress-test environment and observation-quality feature backing.
evidence_location: Noise construction and robustness experiments.

findings: The paper reports 91% HumanEval pass@1 in one configuration versus the cited GPT-4 baseline of 80%; this is not a repository-agent early-warning result.

title: AgentRewardBench: Evaluating Automatic Evaluations of Web Agent Trajectories
history: Submission history From: Xing Han Lù [ view email ] [v1] Fri, 11 Apr 2025 19:49:22 UTC (1,711 KB) [v2] Mon, 6 Oct 2025 15:46:30 UTC (1,714 KB)
status: arXiv preprint; peer review not independently confirmed
verification: Primary metadata plus full-text method/results reading; not independently reproduced
target: Evaluator validity, success and side effects
summary: Expert reviewers annotate success, side effects and repetition in completed web trajectories. Twelve language-model judges are compared against those labels and conventional rule-based evaluators.
findings: The benchmark has 1,302 trajectories from four agent LLMs. No judge dominates across all five environments; common rule-based checks can undercount success.
design: Evaluator agreement concerns label quality. An expert success label and an executable state verifier each have limits; side effects need a separate outcome.
gap: A monitor may learn benchmark-checker artifacts. Noisy terminal labels can distort both training and alarm calibration.
future: Audit contested outcomes, annotate side effects independently, and run sensitivity analyses under executable and expert labels.
evidence_location: Expert annotation and LLM/rule evaluator comparisons.

title: Model-Based Runtime Monitoring with Interactive Imitation Learning
history: Submission history From: Huihan Liu [ view email ] [v1] Thu, 26 Oct 2023 16:45:44 UTC (3,980 KB)
status: arXiv preprint; peer review not independently confirmed
verification: Primary metadata plus full-text method/results reading; not independently reproduced
target: Future risky states and human assistance
summary: A latent dynamics model simulates future policy actions, and a failure classifier predicts risk. Human interventions provide supervision without requiring dangerous failures; the policy and monitor improve through interactive imitation learning.
findings: Reported success gains are 23% in simulation and 40% on hardware against compared baselines; robot-specific human-workload measures improve as deployment data accumulate.
design: The environment admits learned transition dynamics; human intervention labels reflect perceived risk. It is a cross-domain precedent, not direct tool-language-agent evidence.
gap: Semantic APIs, nondeterministic external services and irreversible actions make reliable language-agent simulation harder than latent robot-state rollout.
future: Use checkpoint/replay where valid and explicit abstention where a tool effect cannot be simulated; audit human-help burden separately.
evidence_location: Dynamics/failure-model design and system-level experiments.

title: On Calibration of Modern Neural Networks
history: Submission history From: Geoff Pleiss [ view email ] [v1] Wed, 14 Jun 2017 17:33:50 UTC (1,825 KB) [v2] Thu, 3 Aug 2017 13:29:46 UTC (1,271 KB)
status: arXiv preprint; peer review not independently confirmed; source record: ICML 2017
verification: Primary metadata plus full-text method/results reading; not independently reproduced
summary: Modern neural classifiers can be confidently wrong. Post-hoc temperature scaling adjusts logits using held-out data, distinguishing probability accuracy from class discrimination.
findings: The study finds temperature scaling effective across evaluated architectures and datasets; it does not establish robustness to arbitrary distribution shift.
design: The methodological evidence predates tool agents. A monotonic calibrator preserves ranking and cannot repair AUROC below chance.
gap: In-domain calibration is not a certificate for a new tool scaffold, and threshold calibration is different from measuring full probabilistic reliability.
future: Report Brier/reliability and decision coverage by deployment; recalibrate only with separate target data and preserve an untouched target test split.
role: Calibration foundation; contextual exception to the 2022 start date.
evidence_location: Calibration metrics and temperature-scaling experiments.
